```{r}
#
# Boger & Firestone (2026), Experiment 4 (shapes <-> mathematical expressions). Results, and
# Methods "Experiment 4": 100 participants completed the study; 2 were excluded for earning the
# reward on fewer than 6 of 12 learning trials, leaving N = 98. On the single transfer trial,
# 63 of 98 (64.3%) chose the option consistent with the reward rule they had learned; exact
# binomial test against 50%, P = .006, 95% CI [54.0%, 73.7%].
#
# The split by direction is not reported in the paper. It is counted from the authors' shared
# data (E04 data_and_analysis/cleaned_data.csv, transfer trials, gotReward by stimType):
# learned on shapes and tested on math, 40 of 63; learned on math and tested on shapes, 23 of 35.
# The two rows sum to the paper's 63 of 98.
original <- tibble(
  direction = c("Shapes → math", "Math → shapes"),
  k         = c(40, 23),   # chose the reward-consistent option on the transfer trial
  n         = c(63, 35)    # analysed participants
)
original_k <- sum(original$k)   # 63
original_n <- sum(original$n)   # 98
original_p <- original_k / original_n
```

# Key statistics

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

One row per study for the key comparison: the original, your Phase 1 replication, and your
Phase 2 extension. The table fills itself in from the data as each phase is exported, using the
analysis code below (open "Show the analysis code"), which is shared by both phases so they are
analysed identically. Edit that code once, here, to match your design and preregistered
exclusion rule. On the scientific-extension track, the Phase 2 row reports the new comparison:
adapt its code and say so in the caption.
:::

```{r}
#| label: analysis-functions
#| code-summary: "Show the analysis code (shared by Phase 1 and Phase 2)"

# Exclusion thresholds, from the original preregistration (AsPredicted #209989, question 6).
min_learning_reward <- 0.5   # rewarded on at least 6 of the 12 learning trials (6/12 passes)
min_rt              <- 200   # trials with a response time below 200 ms are dropped

direction_label <- function(learning_stim) {
  case_when(learning_stim == "shapes" ~ "Shapes → math",
            learning_stim == "math"   ~ "Math → shapes")
}
direction_levels <- c("Shapes → math", "Math → shapes")

# Load one phase's exported data and apply the exclusion rule. Returns NULL if that phase
# has not been exported yet, which is how every section below knows to skip itself.
read_phase <- function(id) {
  dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw", id)
  if (!all(file.exists(file.path(dir, c("participants.csv", "trials.csv"))))) return(NULL)
  participants <- read_csv(file.path(dir, "participants.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
  trials       <- read_csv(file.path(dir, "trials.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
  errors_path  <- file.path(dir, "errors.csv")
  errors <- if (file.exists(errors_path)) read_csv(errors_path, show_col_types = FALSE) else tibble()

  # Columns the analysis needs, so it still runs if nobody has reached a choice trial yet.
  for (col in c("task", "gotReward", "isTransferTrial", "rt", "learningStimType")) {
    if (!col %in% names(trials)) trials[[col]] <- NA
  }
  for (col in c("condition", "learningStimType")) {
    if (!col %in% names(participants)) participants[[col]] <- NA
  }

  # 1. Incomplete datasets are excluded.
  complete <- participants |> filter(completed %in% TRUE)

  choices <- trials |>
    filter(task == "choice", participant_id %in% complete$participant_id) |>
    mutate(gotReward = as.numeric(gotReward), rt = as.numeric(rt),
           isTransferTrial = as.logical(isTransferTrial))

  # 2. Learning criterion, scored on all 12 learning trials before any fast trial is dropped (the order the original notebook uses).
  learning <- choices |>
    filter(!isTransferTrial) |>
    group_by(participant_id) |>
    summarise(learning_reward = mean(gotReward), .groups = "drop")

  # 3. Trials faster than 200 ms are dropped. Each participant has a single transfer trial, so one whose transfer trial is dropped has no key response and leaves the analysis.
  transfer <- choices |>
    filter(isTransferTrial) |>
    transmute(participant_id, transfer_rt = rt, transfer_reward = gotReward,
              direction = direction_label(learningStimType))

  checked <- complete |>
    select(participant_id, condition) |>
    left_join(learning, by = "participant_id") |>
    left_join(transfer, by = "participant_id") |>
    mutate(pass_learning    = !is.na(learning_reward) & learning_reward >= min_learning_reward,
           pass_transfer_rt = !is.na(transfer_rt) & transfer_rt >= min_rt)
  keep <- checked |> filter(pass_learning, pass_transfer_rt)

  list(participants = participants, trials = trials, errors = errors,
       complete = complete, checked = checked, keep = keep,
       n_low_learning  = sum(!checked$pass_learning),
       n_fast_transfer = sum(checked$pass_learning & !checked$pass_transfer_rt),
       n_fast_learning_trials = sum(!choices$isTransferTrial & choices$rt < min_rt &
                                    choices$participant_id %in% keep$participant_id, na.rm = TRUE))
}

# The key comparison's raw counts: of the analysed participants in each transfer direction,
# how many chose the reward-consistent option on the transfer trial (k) out of how many (n).
# Same shape as `original` at the top of the file.
transfer_counts <- function(d) {
  d$keep |>
    mutate(direction = factor(direction, levels = direction_levels)) |>
    group_by(direction, .drop = FALSE) |>
    summarise(k = sum(transfer_reward), n = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(direction = as.character(direction))
}

# The key statistic: the proportion choosing the reward-consistent option on the transfer
# trial, pooled over both directions and both reward rules, with its exact (Clopper-Pearson)
# 95% CI and a two-sided exact binomial test against 50%. This is the original notebook's
# binom.test(63, 98). NULL until there is at least one analysed participant.
binom_ci <- function(counts) {
  k <- sum(counts$k)
  n <- sum(counts$n)
  if (n == 0) return(NULL)
  bt <- binom.test(k, n, p = 0.5, alternative = "two.sided")
  tibble(N = n, k = k, estimate = k / n,
         ci_low = bt$conf.int[1], ci_high = bt$conf.int[2], p = bt$p.value)
}

# Side-by-side figure: any number of studies on the same axes, in the order given. Each
# argument is a counts table like `original`. By default the directions are pooled (the key
# comparison); by_direction = TRUE splits them (exploratory).
comparison_plot <- function(..., by_direction = FALSE) {
  studies <- list(...)
  studies <- studies[!map_lgl(studies, ~ is.null(.x) || sum(.x$n) == 0)]
  df <- imap_dfr(studies, function(counts, study) {
    if (!by_direction) counts <- tibble(direction = "Both directions", k = sum(counts$k), n = sum(counts$n))
    counts |> filter(n > 0) |> mutate(Study = study)
  }) |>
    rowwise() |>
    mutate(p = k / n,
           low = binom.test(k, n)$conf.int[1], high = binom.test(k, n)$conf.int[2]) |>
    ungroup() |>
    mutate(Study = factor(Study, levels = names(studies)),
           direction = factor(direction, levels = c("Both directions", direction_levels)),
           label = sprintf("n = %d", n))
  fills <- setNames(c("grey55", "#1E6E76", "#B8792A")[seq_along(studies)], names(studies))
  dodge <- position_dodge(width = 0.8)
  ggplot(df, aes(x = direction, y = p, fill = Study)) +
    geom_col(position = dodge, width = 0.75) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = low, ymax = high), position = dodge, width = 0.2) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey30") +
    geom_text(aes(y = 0.02, label = label), position = dodge, vjust = 0, size = 3, colour = "white") +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = fills) +
    labs(x = if (by_direction) "Learned on → tested on" else NULL,
         y = "Chose the reward-consistent option\non the transfer trial", fill = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(legend.position = "top")
}

phase1 <- read_phase(experiment_id)
phase2 <- read_phase(experiment_id_phase2)
have_data   <- !is.null(phase1)
have_phase2 <- !is.null(phase2)
```

```{r}
#| label: key-stats
#| echo: false
fmt_row <- function(study, r) {
  if (is.null(r)) {
    return(tibble(Study = study, N = "", `Reward-consistent choices` = "not yet collected",
                  `95% CI` = "", p = ""))
  }
  tibble(Study = study, N = as.character(r$N),
         `Reward-consistent choices` = sprintf("%d (%.1f%%)", r$k, 100 * r$estimate),
         `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.1f%%, %.1f%%]", 100 * r$ci_low, 100 * r$ci_high),
         p = format.pval(r$p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001))
}
bind_rows(
  fmt_row("Original", binom_ci(original)),
  fmt_row("Phase 1: replication", if (have_data) binom_ci(transfer_counts(phase1))),
  fmt_row("Phase 2: extension", if (have_phase2) binom_ci(transfer_counts(phase2)))
) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrllr",
               caption = "Key comparison: analysed participants choosing the reward-consistent option on the transfer trial, both directions pooled. Exact 95% CI; two-sided exact binomial test against 50%.")
```

# Phase 1: Replication

## Introduction

<!-- ::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

One or two paragraphs, no abstract and no literature review: that is in the original paper.
Say what the original study found, which specific finding you are replicating, and why it
matters to you. Write the Introduction and Methods in the past tense, even though you write
them before collecting data.
::: -->

**My Research Interests**

I'm interested in the role of abstraction in human cognition, and in particular, in language. 
Boger & Firestone (2026) explore the idea that there is a shared representation of complexity across domains, and I wonder whether some of the ideas and methods in this paper could be relevant to understanding people's intuitive judgments of complexity and abstraction in language. 
I have been thinking a little bit about the relationship between complexity and abstraction, such that while complexity seems like a component of abstractness, there are many other factors that contribute to how abstract something is. 
And while we might think about the abstractness of a drawing in one way, it is unclear whether people think about it in the same way as they do, for example, an explanation or a mathematical concept. 
So, I think this paper will be a good starting point for thinking about different kinds of abstract representations across domains.


**Original Experiments and Findings**

The authors of the original paper conducted a suite of experiments to test whether there is a shared representation of complexity across domains (e.g., visual, auditory, linguistic, mathematical, tactile).
In one set of experiments (Experiments 1-7), they used a learning transfer paradigm in which participants chose between simple and complex stimuli in order to test whether learned associations with complexity transfer to a novel stimulus class. 
They found that the reward rule people learned in one domain transfers to an unseen domain.
For example, in Experiment 4, 64.3% of participants transferred the rule between shapes and mathematical expressions (p=0.006 in exact binomial test, N=98, 95% CI [54.0%, 73.7%]).
<!-- , and that transfer rates differed across domain pairings. <removed because the wording suggests that they conducted a stat test to test the differences across experiments, which I don't think they did.> -->
They also found that such transfer occurs automatically (Experiment 8), and that there were stable individual differences in aesthetic judgments of complexity across different types of information (Experiment 9).


**Stimuli and Procedure**

In this project, I focused on Experiment 4, which is a reward-learning task consisting of two parts. 
In the first part of the study (learning phase), participants completed 12 trials in which they chose between a simple and complex stimulus (e.g., a shape with few smooth edges vs. one with many sharp edges), shown on the left and right sides of the screen. 
They were rewarded for consistently choosing either the simple or complex option, i.e., they learned which type of stimulus was worth more points (with the correct one being randomly assigned to each participant).
If they chose the correct option, a coin would drop into a piggy bank with a 'ding' sound and they would earn 5 points; if they chose the incorrect option, they would hear a 'buzz' sound and earn 0 points.
In the second part (transfer phase), participants completed one trial in which they chose between a simple and complex stimulus of a different domain (e.g., a mathematical expression with one type of operation vs. one with multiple different operations).
The learning stimulus class was randomly assigned for each participant.
Participants completed the study by answering a brief survey asking them to describe the task, guess the purpose of the study, describe their strategy in each phase, and complete an attention check.


**Challenges**

One potential challenge in replicating this experiment is determining whether the stimuli shown to participants might affect the results. 
In the original study, the authors randomly selected the simple and complex shape pairings for each participant by using a subset of the full stimulus set. 
Similarly, the math expressions were generated on each trial for each participant (under some set of constraints).
Another challenge is that the original effect was somewhat small (it was the smallest out of Experiments 1-4).


**Planned Preregistered Analysis / Statistical Tests**

I will likely preregister an exact binomial test to determine whether the proportion of participants matching the learned rule on the transfer trial is above chance.

**Extension**

Some possible extensions of this study are: improving the instruction wording, increasing the sample size, asking participants what they thought the pattern / rule was, changing the mathematical expression stimulus by "normalizing" the visual components more, e.g., by always only showing options that are on one line (no fractions, super/subscripts, etc.), and operationalizing mathematical complexity differently.
<!-- increasing the number of transfer trials (e.g., to 2 or 3) to see if the finding still holds. -->


## Methods

### Power analysis

<!-- ::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

Report the original effect size, the sample needed for 80%, 90% and 95% power to detect it,
and the sample you chose and why. The table below is computed from the original study's
numbers entered at the top of this file.

Original effects are usually overestimates, so powering to the original effect tends to
produce an underpowered replication. One widely used alternative is to collect 2.5 times the
original sample, which gives 80% power to detect an effect the original study had only 33%
power to detect (Simonsohn, 2015; Experimentology §10.4). Say which approach you used, and
what the course's participant budget allowed.
::: -->

"Overall, 100 participants completed the task. In addition, two participants were excluded for failing to learn the reward rule, and 3 of the 1,274 remaining trials were excluded for speed.  In total, 64.3% of participants transferred the reward rule between the geometric shapes and the mathematical expressions (P = 0.006 in the exact binomial test, N = 98, 95% CI 54.0–73.7%)."

We will recruit $N=145$ participants (after exclusions) because it gives a power of 93% for the original estimate, or about 80% for a 62% rate (i.e., 84% of the original effect), which is a more conservative estimate of the true effect size.


```{r}
#| label: power
# Power of the key test (two-sided exact binomial test against 50%, alpha = .05) at sample
# size n if the true rate of reward-consistent choices is p. Exact power rises in a sawtooth
# as n grows, so the N needed is the smallest n at which power stays at or above the target
# for that n and the next 10.
power_binom <- function(n, p, alpha = 0.05) {
  k <- 0:n
  p_values <- vapply(k, function(x) binom.test(x, n, p = 0.5)$p.value, numeric(1))
  sum(dbinom(k[p_values < alpha], n, p))
}
n_needed <- function(p, target, n_range = 20:400) {
  pw <- vapply(n_range, power_binom, numeric(1), p = p)
  stays <- vapply(seq_along(n_range), function(i) all(pw[i:min(i + 10, length(pw))] >= target), logical(1))
  n_range[which(stays)[1]]
}

planned_n <- 145   # planned analysed participants (stopping rule: until 145 pass the exclusions)

# Effects to plan around: the original estimate; a 62% rate, i.e. 12 of the original's 14.3
# points above chance (84% of the original effect), which the planned N detects with 80% power;
# and safeguard power (Perugini, Gallucci & Costantini, 2014), the lower bound of the original's
# two-sided 60% CI.
safeguard_p <- binom.test(original_k, original_n, conf.level = 0.60)$conf.int[1]
effects <- tibble(
  Effect = c(sprintf("Original estimate: %.1f%%", 100 * original_p),
             sprintf("62%% (%.0f%% of the original effect)", 100 * (0.62 - 0.5) / (original_p - 0.5)),
             sprintf("Safeguard (lower bound of the original 60%% CI): %.1f%%", 100 * safeguard_p)),
  p = c(original_p, 0.62, safeguard_p)
)

effects |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(`80%` = n_needed(p, 0.80), `90%` = n_needed(p, 0.90), `95%` = n_needed(p, 0.95),
         `Power at planned N` = scales::percent(power_binom(planned_n, p), accuracy = 1)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(-p) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = sprintf(
    "Analysed N needed for 80%%, 90%% and 95%% power, and power at the planned N = %d, for the two-sided exact binomial test against 50%% (alpha = .05). The original found %d of %d (%.1f%%).",
    planned_n, original_k, original_n, 100 * original_p))

two_and_half <- ceiling(2.5 * original_n)
```

### Materials

<!-- ::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

All materials. You can quote the original article directly: put the text in quotation marks
and note that it was followed precisely, or quote it and point out the exceptions. Link to the
live experiment above rather than pasting screenshots of every screen.
::: -->

**Shapes.** The geometric shapes were drawn from Sun & Firestone (2022). There were 60 shapes in total, 30 simple and 30 complex. The simple and complex shapes were shuffled separately and randomly paired together for each participant.

**Mathematical expressions.** "The simple and complex mathematical expressions within each trial contained identical terms, and only differed in their operations. 
Both expressions contained four unique integers between 11 and 49. 
The integers were randomly generated, while ensuring they were not divisible by 10 and were not multiples of each other. 
The simple mathematical expression merely added the four terms together, while the complex one included a variety of operations (namely, exponentiation, multiplication and division). 
For example, a simple expression might be $17 + 13 + 24 + 31$, and the accompanying  complex expression would be $\frac{17^{13} \times 24}{31}$." 
The expressions were generated fresh on each trial. 

<!-- "Note that this is just one of many possible ways to operationalize mathematical complexity. 
We designed our stimuli in this manner because they hold many features constant (including the numbers in each expression and the length of each expression) and vary only in the operations used. 
However, we think it is likely that mathematical complexity works in other fashions too. 
For example, perhaps $\sqrt{\pi}$ is more complex than $1 + 1 + 1 − 1$, even though the latter is longer and contains more operations than the former. 
Still, the former may feel more complex because it is harder to compute (we thank a reviewer for prompting this discussion)." -->


### Procedure

<!-- ::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

As for Materials: quote the original where you can and point out the exceptions. Describe the
sequence a participant experiences, from consent to debrief, and how long it takes.
::: -->

"This experiment tested bidirectional transfer between geometric shapes 
and mathematical expressions."

"At the start of the experiment, participants were randomly assigned to be rewarded for selecting either the simple stimulus or the complex stimulus on each learning trial. 
In addition, the learning stimulus class was randomly assigned for each participant (either geometric shapes or [mathematical expressions], with the other stimulus class being the transfer stimulus)."

The study begins with a consent form, followed by instructions for the experiment. 
Participants then completed 12 learning trials. 
"On each trial, participants chose between two options on the screen (left or right) and received feedback regarding their choice. 
If participants chose the correct  option, they  heard  a  'ding'  sound,  and  saw  a  virtual  coin drop into a piggy bank, thus increasing the 'coin bank' by 5 points; 
if participants chose the incorrect option, they heard a negative buzzer 
sound, and saw no change in the coin bank." 
After 12 learning trials, participants were told that the same pattern applies to a new transfer trial, and to take their best guess. 
"[They] completed a single transfer trial in which a new stimulus class was presented. 
This key transfer trial was the main target of our analyses."
The study ends with a brief survey asking participants to describe the task, guess the purpose of the study, describe their strategy in each phase, complete an attention check, and provide feedback about the study. 
Participants were told what the study was about at the end of the study, before being redirected to Prolific.

The study takes about 4 minutes to complete.


### Analysis plan

**Exclusions.** Participants are excluded if they did not complete the study, if they answered

**Key analysis of interest.** Whether the proportion of reward-earning answers on the transfer trial is above-chance, tested with an exact binomial probability test (two-sided) against 0.5, $\alpha = 0.05$. The effect size is the proportion of participants choosing the reward-consistent option on the transfer trial, with a 95% confidence interval.

Note: in the original preregistration ([AsPredicted #209989](https://aspredicted.org/7bh9-86xn.pdf)), the authors asked whether the proportion of reward-earning answers on the transfer trial is "above-chance," but in their analysis, they run a two-sided test. We will follow the original analysis and use a two-sided test.

<!-- "If participants who learn that simple (complex) stimuli of one type are worth more points then choose the simple (complex) stimulus of the other type, this would support our hypothesis." -->


**Exclusions.** Participants will be excluded if they did not complete the study or earned the reward on less than 50% (fewer than 6 of 12) of the learning trials. We will also exclude trials with a response time below 200 ms (learning accuracy is scored before fast trials are dropped).


**Exploratory analyses.** We will also explore whether the proportion of reward-earning answers on the transfer trial differs by transfer direction (shapes to math vs. math to shapes).

### Pilot B: Prolific ($N=10$)

```{r}
#| label: pilot-b
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
# Pilot B summary: dropout, attention check, timing and exclusions. Reads the pilot's own
# export, so it keeps working after `experiment_id` moves to the final id.
pilot_b_id <- "boger2026-e4-pilot-b"
# Anonymous participant_ids of your own test runs (e.g. a completed Prolific Preview), which are left out of the summary. Find them by matching identifiers.csv against Prolific.
pilot_b_test_ids <- c()

pilot_b <- read_phase(pilot_b_id)
if (is.null(pilot_b)) {
  cat("::: {.callout-warning icon=false}\n## No Pilot B data yet\n\n",
      "Export with `npm run export -- --experiment ", pilot_b_id,
      " --key <path to your key>` and render again.\n:::\n", sep = "")
} else {
  pb_p <- pilot_b$participants |> filter(!participant_id %in% pilot_b_test_ids)
  pb_c <- pb_p |> filter(completed %in% TRUE)
  pb_checked <- pilot_b$checked |> filter(participant_id %in% pb_c$participant_id)
  pb_keep    <- pilot_b$keep    |> filter(participant_id %in% pb_c$participant_id)

  # Last screen each non-completer reached, e.g. "instructions" or "choice".
  left_at <- pilot_b$trials |>
    filter(participant_id %in% pb_p$participant_id[!pb_p$completed %in% TRUE]) |>
    group_by(participant_id) |>
    slice_max(trial_index, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
    ungroup() |>
    count(task)
  left_at_text <- if (nrow(left_at) == 0) "" else
    paste(sprintf("%s: %d", left_at$task, left_at$n), collapse = ", ")

  turned_away <- pb_p |> filter(device_supported %in% FALSE)
  minutes <- as.numeric(difftime(as.POSIXct(pb_c$ended_at, format = "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%OS", tz = "UTC"),
                                 as.POSIXct(pb_c$started_at, format = "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%OS", tz = "UTC"),
                                 units = "mins"))
  learning <- na.omit(pb_checked$learning_reward) * 12
  sum_ok <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(pb_c$sumCheck)) %in% 2

  tibble(
    Measure = c("Sessions started",
                "Turned away (phone or tablet)",
                "Left before finishing (desktop)",
                "Completed",
                "Answered attention check (\"What is 1 + 1?\") correctly",
                "Completion time, minutes: mean (range)",
                "Learning trials rewarded, of 12: mean (range)",
                "Excluded: fewer than 6 of 12 learning trials rewarded",
                sprintf("Excluded: transfer response faster than %d ms", min_rt),
                "Analyzed"),
    Value = c(nrow(pb_p),
              nrow(turned_away),
              sum(!pb_p$completed %in% TRUE & !pb_p$device_supported %in% FALSE),
              nrow(pb_c),
              sprintf("%d of %d", sum(sum_ok), nrow(pb_c)),
              if (length(minutes)) sprintf("%.1f (%.1f-%.1f)", mean(minutes), min(minutes), max(minutes)) else "",
              if (length(learning)) sprintf("%.1f (%d-%d)", mean(learning), min(learning), max(learning)) else "",
              sum(!pb_checked$pass_learning),
              sum(pb_checked$pass_learning & !pb_checked$pass_transfer_rt),
              nrow(pb_keep)),
    Note = c("", "", if (nzchar(left_at_text)) paste("Last screen reached:", left_at_text) else "",
             rep("", 7))
  ) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = sprintf("Pilot B (`%s`).", pilot_b_id)) |>
    print()

  # Free-text answers, to check that participants understood the task.
  # cat("\n")
  # pb_c |>
  #   select(any_of(c("taskGuess", "purposeGuess", "strategyLearn", "strategyTransfer", "commentText"))) |>
  #   mutate(across(everything(), ~ replace_na(str_squish(as.character(.x)), ""))) |>

  #                   `Strategy, learning` = "strategyLearn", `Strategy, transfer` = "strategyTransfer",
  #                   `Comments` = "commentText"))) |>
  #   knitr::kable(caption = "Pilot B: free-text answers, completed participants.") |>
  #   print()
}
```

```{r}
#| label: funnel
#| eval: !expr have_data
# Attrition and exclusion by transfer direction. Participants who left before the experiment
# assigned them a direction are counted under "Not assigned".
funnel_levels <- c("Started", "Completed", "Passed the learning criterion",
                   "Transfer response at least 200 ms (analysed)")
with_direction <- function(ids) {
  participants |>
    filter(participant_id %in% ids) |>
    mutate(direction = coalesce(direction_label(learningStimType), "Not assigned"))
}
funnel <- bind_rows(
  with_direction(participants$participant_id) |> mutate(step = funnel_levels[1]),
  with_direction(complete$participant_id)     |> mutate(step = funnel_levels[2]),
  with_direction(checked$participant_id[checked$pass_learning]) |> mutate(step = funnel_levels[3]),
  with_direction(keep$participant_id)         |> mutate(step = funnel_levels[4])
) |>
  mutate(step = factor(step, levels = funnel_levels),
         direction = factor(direction, levels = c(direction_levels, "Not assigned"))) |>
  count(step, direction, .drop = FALSE) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = direction, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)
if (all(funnel$`Not assigned` == 0)) funnel$`Not assigned` <- NULL
funnel |>
  mutate(Total = rowSums(across(-step))) |>
  rename(Step = step) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Participants at each step, by transfer direction (the stimulus class learned on, then tested on). Differences between directions in attrition or exclusion are a threat to validity and should be discussed.")
```

```{r}
if (phase1$n_fast_learning_trials > 0) {

              phase1$n_fast_learning_trials, min_rt))
}
```

## Results

### Data preparation

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

Data preparation follows the analysis plan. Loading and exclusions are done by the shared

the data beyond that.

### Confirmatory analysis

```{r}
#| label: confirmatory
#| eval: !expr have_data
# Key analysis: two-sided exact binomial test of the number of analysed participants who chose
# the reward-consistent option on the transfer trial, against 50%, both directions and both
# reward rules pooled (as in the original, binom.test(63, 98)).
counts <- transfer_counts(phase1)
k <- sum(counts$k)
n <- sum(counts$n)

if (n > 0) {
  print(binom.test(k, n, p = 0.5, alternative = "two.sided"))
} else {
  message("Binomial test not run: no participants in the analysis set yet.")
}
```

### Replication assessment

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

Judge the replication on effect sizes, not only on whether the key test is significant. Compare
the replication estimate and its interval with the original: does the interval exclude chance
(50%), and does it include the original estimate? A significant result much smaller than the
original, or a non-significant result whose interval still includes the original effect, are both
informative and should be reported as such (Experimentology §3.2).
:::

```{r}
#| label: comparison
#| eval: !expr have_data
orig <- binom_ci(original)
rep  <- binom_ci(counts)

if (!is.null(rep)) {
  bind_rows(orig |> mutate(Study = "Original"), rep |> mutate(Study = "Phase 1: replication")) |>
    transmute(Study, N,
              `Reward-consistent choices` = sprintf("%d (%.1f%%)", k, 100 * estimate),
              `Above chance` = sprintf("%+.1f points", 100 * (estimate - 0.5)),
              `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.1f%%, %.1f%%]", 100 * ci_low, 100 * ci_high),
              p = format.pval(p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001)) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Effect size: percentage choosing the reward-consistent option on the transfer trial, and its distance above chance (50%). Exact 95% CI.")
} else {
  message("Replication effect size not computed yet: need at least one analysed participant.")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: comparison-verdict
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
if (!is.null(rep)) {
  excludes_chance <- rep$ci_low > 0.5 | rep$ci_high < 0.5
  includes_orig   <- orig$estimate >= rep$ci_low & orig$estimate <= rep$ci_high
  cat(sprintf(
    "The replication's 95%% interval %s chance (50%%) and %s the original estimate of %.1f%%. ",
    if (excludes_chance) "excludes" else "includes",
    if (includes_orig) "includes" else "does not include",
    100 * orig$estimate))
  cat("These two facts are the starting point for the summary in the Discussion, not the conclusion.\n")
}
```

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance: show the original next to your replication

**Every report should have a figure that puts the original finding and your replication side by
side.** It is the single most informative thing in a replication report: a reader can see at a
glance whether the effect came back, and how its size compares. Make it however you can, in
roughly this order of preference:

1. **Replot both from numbers.** Enter the original's summary statistics (means or proportions,
   with SDs, SEs or CIs, and Ns) in the original-study chunk at the top of this file, and plot
   them on the same axes as yours. That is what the demo figure below does.
2. **Replot the original from its data**, if the authors shared it or it is in an open
   repository, using exactly the same plotting code as for your own data.
3. **Show the original figure as an image** next to yours if neither is possible. Save a
   screenshot of it, for example as `writeup/images/original-figure.png`, and lay the two out
   in columns:

   ````markdown
   ::: {layout-ncol=2}
   ![Original: Tversky & Kahneman (1981), Figure 1](images/original-figure.png)

   ```{{r}}
   # your replication plot here
   ```
   :::
   ````

Whichever you choose, use the same measure, scale, condition order and error-bar meaning for
both panels, label which is which, and cite the source of the original values or figure in the
caption. If the original reported no variability, say so rather than leaving it out silently.
:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-comparison
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| fig-cap: "Percentage of analysed participants choosing the reward-consistent option on the transfer trial, both directions pooled: original study (Boger & Firestone, 2026, Experiment 4; 63 of 98) and Phase 1 replication. Error bars are exact 95% confidence intervals; the dashed line is chance (50%)."
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4
comparison_plot(Original = original, `Phase 1: replication` = counts)
```

Any follow-up analyses (optional). Label them clearly as exploratory: they were not planned, so
they generate hypotheses rather than test them.

```{r}
#| label: exploratory-direction
#| eval: !expr have_data
# Transfer by direction (learned on shapes and tested on math, or the reverse). Exploratory:
# no test is run, and the original paper does not report this split; the original counts are
# from the authors' shared data (see the original-study chunk at the top).
by_direction <- bind_rows(
  original |> mutate(Study = "Original"),
  counts   |> mutate(Study = "Phase 1: replication")
) |>
  filter(n > 0) |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(ci = list(binom.test(k, n)$conf.int)) |>
  ungroup()

by_direction |>
  transmute(Study, Direction = direction, N = n,
            `Reward-consistent choices` = sprintf("%d (%.1f%%)", k, 100 * k / n),
            `95% CI` = map_chr(ci, ~ sprintf("[%.1f%%, %.1f%%]", 100 * .x[1], 100 * .x[2]))) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Exploratory: reward-consistent choices on the transfer trial by direction (the stimulus class learned on, then tested on). Exact 95% CIs.")
```

### Summary of replication attempt

## Guidance

Open with one paragraph summarizing the result of the key analysis and your assessment of
whether the original finding replicated, partially replicated, or failed to replicate. Base
that judgment on the replication assessment above: the size of the effect relative to the
original, not just the p value.

### Commentary

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

Open-ended commentary, none of it long: (a) what the exploratory analyses suggest; (b) what the

challenges raised by you or the original authors.
:::

# Phase 2: Extension

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance: choosing your extension

Follow the Extension guidelines page on Canvas. In brief:

- **By default the extension is a best-practices modification of your Phase 1 experiment.** If
  your replication did not succeed, it is a **rescue**: address the plausible reasons for the
  failure. If it did succeed, it is an **upgrade**: make the estimate more precise. Typical
  changes are better or more reliable measurement, more trials, a within-participant design
  where that is legitimate, comprehension and manipulation checks, clearer instructions, or a
  larger or better-targeted sample.
- **If your scientific extension pitch was approved at Milestone 3 and your replication
  succeeded, propose that instead:** the original conditions rerun unchanged, plus the one
  added condition or manipulation, with a power analysis for the new comparison.
- On either track you may add exploratory measures **at the end** of the study.
- Every change is listed and tagged by category below; everything else stays identical.

State your track on the line below, and delete the others.
:::

**Track:** Best-practices upgrade / Best-practices rescue / Scientific extension (approved at Milestone 3)

## Rationale

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

One or two paragraphs. For a rescue: what are the plausible reasons Phase 1 did not reproduce the
original result, and how does each change address one of them? For an upgrade: where is the
Phase 1 estimate least precise or least trustworthy, and how will the changes improve it? For a
scientific extension: what question does the added condition answer, and why does it follow from
the original finding?
:::

## Changes from Phase 1

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

Every change from the Phase 1 experiment, one per row, each tagged with a category: Measurement,
Trials, Design, Checks, Instructions, Sample, Added condition (scientific track only), or
Exploratory measure (end of study only). If it is not in this table, it does not change: same
materials, wording, procedure, exclusion rule and analysis. The rows below are examples for the
demo; replace them with yours.
:::

| # | Category | Phase 1 | Phase 2 | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Sample | 27 analysed participants | 300 analysed participants (150 per frame) | Phase 1's interval was too wide to distinguish the original effect from a much smaller one. |
| 2 | Checks | No comprehension check | After the choice, participants say how many people are at risk (600) | Confirms participants read the scenario; failures are reported, and excluded only if preregistered. |
| 3 | Exploratory measure | None | At the end: "How confident are you in your choice?" (1–7) | Exploratory only; collected after every confirmatory measure. |

Everything not listed above is identical to Phase 1.

## Power and sample

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Guidance

Justify the Phase 2 sample, and **state how you expect the estimate and its precision to compare
with Phase 1**. For an upgrade, plan the sample around the confidence interval you want; for a
rescue, around the power to detect the original effect, or the smallest effect you would still
consider a successful replication; for a scientific extension, around the power to detect the new
comparison. Set `phase2_n` in the code below; the table uses Phase 1's estimate if you
have it and the original's otherwise.
:::

```{r}
#| label: phase2-power
phase2_n <- planned_n   # placeholder: planned analysed participants in Phase 2; set when you plan it

p1_stats <- if (have_data) binom_ci(transfer_counts(phase1))
basis <- if (!is.null(p1_stats)) {
  list(p = p1_stats$estimate, source = "Phase 1")
} else {
  list(p = original_p, source = "the original study")
}

# Expected exact 95% CI half-width at n if the true rate is basis$p.
half_width <- function(n) {
  ci <- binom.test(round(basis$p * n), n)$conf.int
  (ci[2] - ci[1]) / 2
}

rows <- tibble(
  Study = c(if (!is.null(p1_stats)) "Phase 1 (actual)", "Phase 2 (planned)"),
  `N analysed` = c(if (!is.null(p1_stats)) p1_stats$N, phase2_n),
  `95% CI half-width` = c(if (!is.null(p1_stats)) sprintf("±%.1f points", 100 * (p1_stats$ci_high - p1_stats$ci_low) / 2),
                          sprintf("±%.1f points (expected)", 100 * half_width(phase2_n)))
)
knitr::kable(rows, caption = sprintf("Precision of the key estimate, Phase 2 expected values based on %s.", basis$source))

tibble(
  `Rate to detect` = c(sprintf("Original: %.1f%%", 100 * original_p),
                       if (!is.null(p1_stats)) sprintf("Phase 1: %.1f%%", 100 * p1_stats$estimate),
                       sprintf("Half the original effect: %.1f%%", 100 * (0.5 + (original_p - 0.5) / 2))),
  `Power at planned N` = scales::percent(c(
    power_binom(phase2_n, original_p),
    if (!is.null(p1_stats)) power_binom(phase2_n, p1_stats$estimate),
    power_binom(phase2_n, 0.5 + (original_p - 0.5) / 2)
  ), accuracy = 1)
) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = sprintf("Power of the Phase 2 key test (two-sided exact binomial test against 50%%, alpha = .05) at N = %d analysed.", phase2_n))
```
